title: Writing About a Victorian Novel
context:
Ibrahim: I finished rereading it last night. The ending still surprised me, even the second time.
Chloe: Me too. I stayed up until two in the morning. Right, before Dr Hughes comes, let's agree what we think of the main characters in Great Expectations. Pip first.
Ibrahim: He changes the most, doesn't he? He starts as a village boy and ends up as someone completely different.
Chloe: Yes. Although I'd say Estella changes more at the end. No, on reflection it's Pip, because the whole book is about his development.
Ibrahim: And Estella?
Chloe: She's cruel, but Miss Havisham brought her up to be cruel, so it's hard to blame her.
Ibrahim: Miss Havisham herself is stuck in the past. She's still wearing her wedding dress decades later.
Chloe: Magwitch is the most interesting. First he looks frightening, then he turns out to be much more complicated. He's even kind.
Ibrahim: And Joe is the one person who never lies. He's the most honest of them all.
Chloe: I thought he was only a minor figure, but you're right, he matters a great deal.
Dr Hughes: Hello, both. I've read your essay plan. The introduction names your topic, but it doesn't state an argument. You need one clear sentence saying what you will prove.
Chloe: Should the plot summary come at the end instead?
Dr Hughes: No, drop it altogether. Now, the first body paragraph. It makes a good point, but there's hardly any evidence from the text. You need at least three quotations.
Ibrahim: We have plenty of quotations in the second paragraph.
Dr Hughes: They are far too long, some of them half a page. Trim each to a line or two. The conclusion is too general. Saying that Dickens was a great writer tells me nothing. Say what your argument has shown. The title, though, is fine as it is. Don't change it.
Ibrahim: Next, the sources. The review from 1861 is interesting, but it was written so long ago that it doesn't reflect how we read the book today.
Chloe: The biography is too general. It's mainly about his whole life, with only a few pages on this novel.
Ibrahim: The film adaptation changes the ending, so it contradicts the book. I wouldn't use it as evidence.
Chloe: There's a critic's article I like, but it only covers the first half of the novel.
Ibrahim: I wondered if she was biased, but she seems balanced. And the textbook you mentioned is lovely, but the library doesn't have it.
Dr Hughes: Let's sort out the practical side. Chloe, will you find the original review?
Chloe: I can try.
Ibrahim: Don't bother, Dr Hughes has a copy.
Dr Hughes: That's right. I'll send it to you. Chloe, book a study room for Thursday. Ibrahim, order the textbook from another library.
Ibrahim: Okay. And who reads the draft?
Dr Hughes: I will. Chloe's sister has offered to proofread it, and the librarian will print the copies for the seminar.
Dr Hughes: The seminar is on Friday at ten, so please arrive a few minutes early to set up. And remember that a good essay answers the question it is asked, not the one you wish you had been given.
Chloe: Brilliant, thank you. We will keep that in mind.
